title: Minimize String Length
statement:
You may change the string `s` with either of two moves, as many times as you like (zero times is fine):

- Pick a position `i` and let `c = s[i]`. If `c` also occurs somewhere before `i`, delete the occurrence of `c` nearest to `i` on its left.
- Pick a position `i` and let `c = s[i]`. If `c` also occurs somewhere after `i`, delete the occurrence of `c` nearest to `i` on its right.

After a deletion the remaining characters close up. Return the smallest length that `s` can be brought down to.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Each move deletes one copy of a character, but only when another copy of the same character remains to point at it. So a character can never vanish entirely, while any character with two or more copies can always lose one more (pick one copy and delete its nearest twin). Following the moves until none is possible would work, but it is simpler to see where they end: exactly one copy of every distinct character survives. The answer is just the number of distinct characters, which a hash set counts in one pass.

## Approach

1. Create an empty set `seen`.
2. Add every character `ch` of `s` to it; duplicates are ignored by the set.
3. Return `seen.size`, the number of distinct characters.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aaabc"`:

- `a` is added: `seen = {a}`. The next two `a`s change nothing.
- `b` is added: `seen = {a, b}`.
- `c` is added: `seen = {a, b, c}`.

`seen.size` is `3`, matching the final string `"abc"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over `s`.
- Space: O(1): the set never holds more than 26 letters.

## Pitfalls

- The positions of the duplicates do not matter (`"azzzza"` still ends with 2 letters); there is no need to simulate the moves.
- Do not count only adjacent duplicates, as in the "remove adjacent duplicates" problems: `"abab"` shrinks to length 2.
- The answer is at least 1, since `s` is non-empty and its last copy of each letter can never be deleted.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | set of the distinct characters met so far |
| `ch` | the current character of `s` |

narration.1: The moves can remove every repeated copy but never the last copy of a letter.
narration.2: The set will hold each distinct character once.
narration.4: Visit every character of the string.
narration.5: Adding a character that is already in the set changes nothing, so only new letters count.
narration.6: The loop ends once every character has been recorded.
narration.7: One copy of each distinct letter must survive and all others can be deleted, so the set size is the answer.
